strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: selecting segmentation models for an unlabelled target microscopy dataset without source data or fine-tuning. Supporting both semantic and instance segmentation makes the application relevant to microscopy model banks.

The estimator is simple and inexpensive: compare an unperturbed prediction with a perturbed prediction, restrict scoring to predicted foreground, and aggregate across images. Input perturbations support black-box models, while feature dropout supports models with accessible intermediate layers.

The reported results are promising across multiple microscopy datasets and modalities. Feature-based CTE achieves mean Kendall correlations of 1.00 and 0.83 for semantic mitochondria and nuclei segmentation, and 0.87 and 0.76 for instance cell and nuclei segmentation, respectively.

The manuscript clearly connects the approach to prior work on invariance, uncertainty, and generalization. Comparing hard versus soft consistency and exploring dropout strength provide useful initial evidence about design choices.
weaknesses: Under the default Algorithms/General assessment, the methodological advance is modest: prediction consistency under perturbation is established, and the proposed segmentation scores adapt Effective Invariance or use existing IoU and Rand measures. This adaptation could still support a valuable contribution, but the experimental evidence does not yet adequately establish its advantage or generality.

The comparisons do not convincingly support the state-of-the-art claim. The only external comparator, CCFV, targets transferability after fine-tuning rather than zero-shot performance, a mismatch the authors acknowledge. There are no comparisons with simple unlabelled-target confidence, entropy, or uncertainty scores. Likewise, the absence of a dedicated instance-transferability method does not preclude constructing meaningful baseline rankings.

The model banks are small—three to seven candidates—and consist predominantly of U-Nets trained by the authors using similar protocols. Training explicitly includes the same augmentation types used for consistency evaluation. Although two public cell models are included, the experiments provide limited evidence for heterogeneous model zoos with unknown training augmentations, architectures, and robustness properties. Perfect ordering among three mitochondria models is encouraging but insufficient to establish broad reliability.

Important implementation details are missing: the perturbation strengths used for the main tables and their selection procedure, input normalization and augmentation composition, segmentation thresholds, the Rand-score alpha parameter, and the conversion of BCEDice-trained U-Net outputs into instances. Exact dataset sizes, splits, and training settings are also insufficiently documented, and no code availability statement is provided. These omissions materially hinder reproduction, especially for instance segmentation.

The evidence for reliable two-pass selection is incomplete. Results use a single random perturbation, while the reported standard deviations summarize variation across target datasets rather than perturbation seeds. The claim that additional perturbations provide no advantage lacks quantitative support. Figure 3 examines only selected transfers, and there is no label-free rule for choosing perturbation strength. Top-model selection accuracy or performance regret would also better establish practical utility than aggregate correlations alone.

The central failure mode—consistent but incorrect predictions—is not investigated. Restricting evaluation to non-empty images does not resolve stable incorrect foreground masks or undefined scores when both predictions are empty. The criterion for excluding empty images is also unclear. Moreover, input-based instance ranking is substantially weaker for cells (mean Kendall correlation 0.54), warranting a more qualified claim about black-box reliability and a discussion of conditions under which consistency is informative.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer vision problem: selecting pretrained segmentation models using unlabelled target images without source training data. This is practically relevant to microscopy model zoos.

The estimator is simple and inexpensive, requiring one original and one perturbed inference pass per image in the reported experiments. Input perturbations support black-box access, while feature perturbations support models with accessible intermediate layers.

Experiments cover semantic and instance segmentation across electron and light microscopy. The reported feature-based ranking correlations are encouraging: average Kendall tau is 1.00 for mitochondria semantic segmentation, 0.83 for nuclei semantic segmentation, and 0.87 and 0.76 for cell and nuclei instance segmentation, respectively.
The manuscript clearly connects its approach to prior work on invariance and uncertainty, compares hard and soft consistency measures, and includes an initial perturbation-strength analysis.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not adequately establish reliability in the heterogeneous model-zoo setting motivating the paper. Each target has only 3–7 candidate models, predominantly author-trained 2D U-Nets using similar training procedures. Only two public models are added for cell segmentation. Because training uses the same augmentation types as consistency evaluation, rankings could partly reflect shared training choices; robustness across substantially different architectures and augmentation histories remains untested.

Comparative evidence is insufficient for the state-of-the-art claim. The main external baseline, CCFV, estimates transferability after fine-tuning rather than zero-shot performance, a mismatch the manuscript itself acknowledges. CTE-EI is a useful comparison, but additional unsupervised confidence, uncertainty, or prediction-agreement baselines are needed. The absence of prior instance-transferability estimators does not preclude adapting simple baselines to that setting.

Critical details of the unsupervised procedure are missing. The main experiments do not specify the chosen dropout rate, input perturbation strengths and sampling distributions, or how these choices are made without target labels. Figure 3 examines only one semantic and one instance target and provides no quantitative sensitivity summary. This leaves the reproducibility and practical robustness of the central ranking procedure uncertain.

The statistical evidence is limited. Reported standard deviations describe variation across targets, rather than repeated training or perturbation trials. With small candidate banks and a single stochastic perturbation, ranking stability needs direct measurement. The claim that averaging additional perturbations offers no advantage is unsupported by reported results. Top-model selection accuracy or performance regret would also make the practical significance of the correlations clearer.

Consistency can reward stable but incorrect predictions, and the paper neither characterizes this failure mode nor states conditions under which consistency should track accuracy. Foreground restriction helps address background dominance but does not resolve consistently wrong foreground masks; handling of empty predicted unions is unspecified. Evaluation is restricted to non-empty images without explaining how that restriction is determined in the intended unlabelled setting.

Reproduction of the experiments is difficult from the supplied manuscript: exact split sizes, preprocessing, training hyperparameters, and the conversion of BCEDice-trained U-Net outputs into instance masks are not provided. The Rand-score parameter alpha is also unspecified, and no code or checkpoint availability statement is given.

Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the methodological advance is modest: existing perturbation-consistency ideas are combined with prediction IoU or an established Rand score. This could still support a valuable empirical contribution, but the current comparisons and robustness evidence are insufficient. Claims that input and feature perturbations yield similar results also need qualification: cell-instance Kendall tau drops from 0.87 to 0.54 with input perturbations in Table 2.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful, well-motivated problem: selecting segmentation models without source data, target annotations, or fine-tuning. This is particularly relevant to microscopy model zoos.

The estimator is simple and computationally attractive, requiring one original and one perturbed inference pass. Input perturbations support black-box models, while feature dropout provides an alternative when intermediate layers are accessible.

Results span semantic and instance segmentation across mitochondria, nuclei, and cells. Reported feature-based Kendall correlations are encouraging: 1.00 and 0.83 for semantic segmentation, and 0.87 and 0.76 for instance segmentation.

The paper acknowledges its foundations in consistency and uncertainty estimation. Comparing hard and soft agreement measures, restricting agreement to predicted foreground, and examining dropout strength provide useful empirical insight.
weaknesses: The comparative evidence is insufficient to establish the claimed state of the art. The only external baseline, CCFV, predicts fine-tuned transfer performance rather than zero-shot performance, a mismatch the authors acknowledge. Simple unsupervised alternatives such as prediction confidence, entropy, or dropout variance are missing. Instance segmentation also warrants baseline comparisons despite the claimed novelty of its problem setting.

The model banks contain only three to seven candidates and predominantly use author-trained 2D U-Nets with similar training procedures. Training explicitly includes the same augmentation types used for evaluation. Consequently, the experiments provide limited evidence that consistency produces comparable scores across independently trained models with different architectures and robustness properties; only two external cell models are included.

Important reproduction and deployment details are absent: the default dropout rate, input perturbation strengths and their selection without target labels, intensity normalization, segmentation thresholds, instance-generation postprocessing, and the alpha parameter in Equation 6. Exact dataset sizes and splits are also unspecified. These choices can materially affect the reported rankings.

Consistency need not imply correctness: a systematically wrong but stable segmentation can receive a high score. Foreground restriction addresses background dominance but does not resolve this failure mode, and handling of two empty predictions is unspecified. Evaluation excludes empty images or patches without explaining how these are identified in the label-free setting.

The statistical evidence is limited to averages and variation across target datasets. There are no repeated perturbation trials or training seeds to establish ranking stability, and the assertion that additional perturbation runs offer no advantage is not supported quantitatively. Top-choice accuracy or performance regret would better establish practical model-selection utility. Input-based cell ranking is also substantially weaker, with mean Spearman correlation 0.57, qualifying the broad black-box applicability claim.

Under the default Algorithms/General category, originality primarily lies in adapting existing consistency measures to this selection setting: the semantic hard score is IoU, and the instance score is an established Rand measure. This can be valuable, but the limited comparisons and reproducibility gaps leave the scientific case slightly below the acceptance threshold despite promising initial results.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting biomedical segmentation models without target annotations or source data. Its applicability to instance segmentation and models with different post-processing pipelines is particularly valuable.

CTE is simple and inexpensive, comparing original and perturbed segmentation outputs with only two inference passes per image in the reported configuration. Input perturbations also permit evaluation without access to model internals.

The empirical coverage is substantial: microscopy semantic and instance segmentation, 42-class 3D dental segmentation, and post-UDA ranking. Table 1 reports mean Spearman correlations of approximately 0.77–0.86, substantially exceeding Transfer Score; Table 2 demonstrates strong overall ranking on ToothFairy2.

The supplementary perturbation sweeps and experiments with publicly available models strengthen the practical case. The paper appropriately credits consistency and uncertainty-estimation predecessors and candidly illustrates stable-but-incorrect predictions and task ambiguity.
weaknesses: Consistency measures stability rather than correctness. This is an observed limitation, not merely a hypothetical counterexample: post-Mean-Teacher ranking on VNC has Spearman correlation 0.24, and supplementary examples show high consistency despite poor cell segmentation. Calling the estimator 'assumption-free' is therefore excessive. Incorrectly segmenting another structure during mitochondria adaptation does not itself establish that the source and target tasks differ.

The label-free configuration protocol is insufficiently specified. The paper explores multiple perturbations, strengths, dropout locations, and consistency measures, but does not clearly explain how the reported configurations are selected without target labels. Sensitivity is sometimes substantial: in Table 28, BBBC039 Kendall correlation varies from 0.20 to 0.80 across Gaussian-noise ranges. A fixed configuration evaluated on held-out domains would strengthen the central unsupervised claim.

Global rank correlations do not directly establish reliable best-model selection. Top-choice accuracy, performance regret relative to the best candidate, and repeated-perturbation uncertainty are missing. This matters particularly for banks of only five to eight models and for distinguishing closely performing candidates. Supplementary Section 8.2 also selects targets partly for differentiated transfer performance, limiting conclusions about harder model-selection settings.

Algorithmic originality is modest: the method combines established perturbation-consistency ideas with existing overlap and partition-comparison metrics. Its main value is the segmentation application and empirical validation. Comparisons against simple confidence/entropy scores, prediction variance, and alternative instance-consistency measures would better establish the benefit of the specific design; the absence of an established instance-ranking method does not preclude such controls.

Reproducibility requires additional detail. The manuscript does not clearly specify class-aggregation weights, empty-mask handling, the ARS alpha parameter, or input normalization relative to noise magnitudes. Equation 3 also describes the contingency-table entry p_ij as a same-label probability, which is misleading for arbitrarily numbered instances. These are correctable issues, but some directly affect rankings.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting biomedical segmentation models without target annotations or source data. Its output-based formulation accommodates heterogeneous architectures and instance-generation pipelines, making it relevant to model repositories.

The empirical coverage is substantial: semantic and instance segmentation, multiple microscopy modalities, 3D ToothFairy2 segmentation, public pretrained models, and post-UDA evaluation. Table 1 reports mean Kendall correlations of 0.62–0.77 for CTE, substantially exceeding the unsupervised Transfer Score baseline.

Instance segmentation is a particularly useful extension. Adapted Rand consistency avoids arbitrary instance-label correspondence, and Table 4 reports mean Spearman correlations of 0.83–0.85. The public-model experiment provides additional evidence beyond models trained by the authors.

The method is simple and inexpensive, requiring two inference passes per image in the reported configuration. The supplementary perturbation sweeps and explicit discussion of stable-but-incorrect predictions strengthen the empirical contribution. Under Algorithms/General, these merits support a borderline acceptance despite the concerns below.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: the estimator combines established perturbation-consistency ideas with existing segmentation agreement metrics. Although the paper appropriately acknowledges these foundations, comparisons against simple confidence/entropy scores and prediction-variance uncertainty estimators would better establish what the proposed formulation adds beyond Transfer Score and supervised transferability metrics.

The evaluation primarily establishes global rank correlation rather than successful selection of the best model. Several candidate banks contain only five to eight models, and the supplementary dataset description explicitly selects targets partly for differentiated transfer performance. Top-1 selection regret, top-k recovery, and evaluation among similarly performing candidates would better substantiate the intended deployment benefit.

The supplementary sweeps are useful, but there is no clear label-free rule for choosing perturbation type, strength, or dropout placement on a new target. These choices vary across experiments, and no separate development/evaluation protocol is described. Consequently, the reported results do not fully establish performance with a configuration fixed before observing target-label correlations.

Consistency cannot distinguish robust correctness from robust error. This is demonstrated, rather than merely hypothetical: Table 3 gives Kendall correlations of only 0.21 and 0.39 on VNC after Mean Teacher and AdaBN adaptation. Describing erroneous segmentation of other structures as violating task alignment is unconvincing when the source and target tasks are both mitochondria segmentation. The 'assumption-free' characterization in Section 3.2 should therefore be qualified, and the frequency and selection consequences of these failures quantified.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite detailed dataset descriptions. The manuscript does not clearly specify input normalization for noise magnitudes, class-aggregation weights, empty-mask handling, or the ARS alpha setting. Repeated perturbation seeds and uncertainty on selection outcomes are also absent; the reported across-dataset standard deviations do not establish the stability of the two-pass ranking procedure.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: selecting biomedical segmentation models without target annotations or source training data. Evaluated as an Algorithms/General contribution, its main value is a simple, broadly applicable estimator supported by substantial empirical evaluation.

Computing consistency in the final segmentation space enables comparison across architectures and instance-generation pipelines. The Adapted Rand Score formulation handles arbitrary instance identifiers and supports comparisons between specialist models, µSAM, and Cellpose-SAM. Input perturbations also permit ranking without access to internal model features.

The experimental coverage is strong: semantic and instance segmentation, electron and light microscopy, multiclass 3D CBCT, and post-UDA evaluation. Table 1 reports mean Spearman correlations of approximately 0.77–0.86 for CTE, substantially exceeding Transfer Score. Table 4 reports instance-segmentation correlations of 0.83–0.85, while Table 2 demonstrates strong overall ToothFairy2 rankings.

The method is computationally attractive, requiring an unperturbed and a perturbed inference per image in the reported setting. Supplementary perturbation sweeps provide useful evidence that successful ranking is not confined to one precise parameter value.

The manuscript appropriately credits prior consistency, uncertainty, and transferability methods, and candidly analyzes stable-but-incorrect predictions, post-UDA failures, and cell-versus-nucleus ambiguity. These discussions help establish the method’s practical scope.
weaknesses: The algorithmic novelty is moderate: CTE combines established perturbations with established output-agreement measures, and CTE-EI directly extends Effective Invariance. The comparison would be more convincing with simple unsupervised alternatives such as confidence/entropy, prediction variance, and other output-agreement scores under identical perturbations. The absence of an established instance-transferability method does not preclude such baselines.

Consistency does not establish correctness. This is an observed limitation, not merely a hypothetical one: Table 3 reports VNC Spearman correlations of only 0.24 after Mean Teacher and 0.47 after AdaBN, and the manuscript identifies models that consistently segment incorrect structures. Calling the estimator 'assumption-free' in Section 3.2 is therefore too strong. Models trained for the same intended task can still make systematic semantic errors under domain shift.

The evaluation emphasizes whole-ranking correlations rather than the stated practical goal of selecting the best model. Top-1 selection accuracy, performance loss relative to the oracle, and top-k recall would show whether residual ranking errors matter. This is particularly relevant because several candidate banks contain only five to eight models, and Supplement Section 8.2 explicitly selects targets partly for differentiated model performance.

The perturbation-selection protocol is insufficiently specified for deployment on a new unlabeled target. Different tasks use different strengths and dropout locations, without a clear label-free rule for choosing them. Sensitivity can be material: in Supplement Table 10, DSB2018 CTE-NHD Kendall correlation changes from 0.14 to 0.81 across Gaussian-noise ranges. Fixed settings evaluated on held-out target domains would strengthen the generalization claim.

Reproducibility and uncertainty reporting need improvement. The manuscript does not clearly specify all class-aggregation weights, the ARS alpha setting, empty-mask handling, or image-intensity normalization needed to interpret perturbation magnitudes. The reported standard deviations across datasets do not establish repeatability under random perturbations, especially for the two-inference claim. Repeated-seed results and complete configurations would address these concerns.
